items.abstract_original: Agents for Image Restoration (IR) aim to leverage Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to autonomously perceive image degradation and invoke IR tools. However, existing IR agents typically rely on fine-tuning MLLM parameters to adapt to new IR tasks, leading to catastrophic forgetting of IR knowledge. To address this limitation, we propose a skill-augmented IR agent, dubbed SIR-Agent, that maintains IR knowledge in a scalable skill library and uses Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) to facilitate efficient skill-library evolution. Specifically, we design a Chain Feedback-driven Skill Revision (CFSR) to evolve the skill library. The CFSR analyzes restoration chains to identify and revise weak operations in existing skills. The compatibility of a revised skill with known tasks decides if it replaces the original skill or is appended independently. Furthermore, to advance CFSR's skill-library evolution, we present an RSI-driven skill meta-learning mechanism, which identifies CFSR's inefficient operations and autonomously refines its revision strategy. Extensive experiments across 14 IR benchmarks, covering 6 single-degradation and 8 mixed-degradation scenarios, demonstrate SIR-Agent's superior IR performance. Further evaluation on 7 unseen tasks validates SIR-Agent's generalization to new IR tasks.
items.reason_zh: CFSR 依据真实恢复链中的中间图像、工具调用和质量反馈，替换技能中的工具配置，并用历史输入回放决定覆盖旧技能或新增具有适用条件的条目；技能用于后续任务。另一个元学习环根据修订轨迹改写外部定位、检索、排序及停止规则，经相同验证输入与预算比较后用于后续 CFSR 轮次，因此符合 Harness 改进器自身进化。
items.summary_zh: SIR-Agent 冻结多模态模型，用图像恢复链反馈修订可复用技能中的工具配置，并回放历史输入检查兼容性。系统进一步依据修订轨迹改写外部技能修订规则，将被接受的技能和规则保留到后续任务及改进轮次。
items.summary_en: With its multimodal model frozen, SIR-Agent uses image-restoration execution feedback to revise tool configurations in reusable skills and checks compatibility by replaying prior inputs. It also refines external skill-revision instructions from revision trajectories and retains accepted skills and rules for later tasks and improvement rounds.

items.execution_feedback: Intermediate restored images, candidate tool execution outputs, normalized image-quality metrics, prior-case replay, and measured tool-call/token cost.
items.persistence: Skill library entries support subsequent tasks; accepted revision instructions guide later CFSR runs.

evidence.quote: Building on RSI, we propose an RSI-driven skill meta-learning mechanism for SIR-Agent. CFSR revises restoration skills using chain feedback. Skill meta-learning then uses the revision trajectories to refine CFSR’s rules for subsequent revisions. Both restoration skills and their revision procedure therefore evolve while the MLLM parameters remain frozen.
evidence.purpose: frozen weights and two actual persistent update objects

evidence.quote: The overall architecture of SIR-Agent is shown in Fig. 2 (a). Given a degraded image, the SIR-Agent progressively loads relevant skills from the skill library. The initial skill library is constructed from restoration trajectories, as detailed in Sec. 4.1 . Each skill specifies applicability conditions, ordered operations, and tool configurations. Once candidate skills are collected, the MLLM selects the skill whose applicability conditions match the observed degradations. The SIR-Agent invokes the configured tools in the specified order to obtain the restored image. The restoration trajectory provides CFSR with intermediate images, tool calls, configurations, and feedback to revise the selected skill.
evidence.purpose: executed skills and restoration-chain feedback

evidence.quote: In the skill revision stage of Fig. 2 (a), CFSR generates a patched skill from restoration-chain feedback and validates it on prior cases before updating the skill library. The revised skills support subsequent tasks, while revision trajectories record the update process. RSI-driven skill meta-learning uses the revision trajectories to refine CFSR’s rules for subsequent skill revisions. The two modules are detailed in Secs. 3.2 and 3.3 .
evidence.purpose: cross-task persistence

evidence.quote: Restoration skills enable strategy reuse but may become ineffective when degradation conditions change. Relying only on the final restored image makes it difficult to identify which operation needs revision, because the image reflects the combined effects of all operations. Therefore, we propose Chain Feedback-driven Skill Revision (CFSR), which uses restoration-chain feedback to guide targeted skill revision. As shown in Fig. 2 (b), CFSR comprises patched skill generation, patched skill validation, and skill updates. Patched skill generation takes a skill s s and its restoration trajectory as inputs. The MLLM examines intermediate images and chain feedback to identify suspicious steps. Localization considers residual degradations and the effects of each operation on subsequent steps. Using the restoration trajectory and identified operations, CFSR retrieves the top- K K candidate tools through LlamaIndex [ 25 ] . For each identified operation, CFSR tests candidate tools on the same intermediate input image and compares the restoration quality of their outputs. The best-performing tool is selected for each operation, and the selected replacements form a patched skill s ′ s^{\prime} . The patched skill updates the associated tool configurations while retaining the operation order.
evidence.purpose: actual execution-based tool replacement; operation order retained

Δ ​ Q ¯ \overline{\Delta Q} measures the overall benefit, while R reg R_{\mathrm{reg}} captures losses on individual prior cases. However, a positive Δ ​ Q ¯ \overline{\Delta Q} can hide regressions on individual inputs. Therefore, a patched skill is compatible when Δ ​ Q ¯ > 0 \overline{\Delta Q}>0 and R reg ≤ τ R_{\mathrm{reg}}\leq\tau , where τ \tau is the permitted regression rate. A compatible patch updates the original skill; otherwise, the original skill is retained and the patched skill is added as a new entry with its inferred applicability conditions. CFSR records revision decisions, tool trials, replay outcomes, library updates, and resource usage in a revision trajectory, which RSI-driven skill meta-learning analyzes to improve CFSR’s revision rules.

evidence.quote: Fixed revision rules cannot incorporate lessons from earlier revisions, so CFSR may repeat ineffective edits and redundant tool trials on similar cases. Inspired by RSI [ 47 ] , we design a skill meta-learning mechanism that improves CFSR’s external revision instructions using recorded trajectories, as illustrated in Fig. 3 . The MLLM examines the trajectories to connect inefficient revision steps with the instructions that guide them. For example, repeated edits without quality gains motivate changes to step priorities. Low-yield trials motivate adjustments to tool retrieval and ranking, while stalled search guides changes to candidate expansion, operation switching, or stopping. The resulting proposals target external revision rules, including those for step localization, tool selection, and revision control. To evaluate the proposals, CFSR is run with the current and candidate rules on the same validation cases and starting skills, using the same tool library and budget limits. Restoration gain is the mean Q Q improvement over the starting skills; revision cost is measured by actual tool calls and MLLM token usage. items.title: RemoteEvolver: Expanding Earth Observation Capabilities through Agent Harness Evolution

identity.submission_history: Submission history From: Shengxiang Xu [ view email ] [v1] Fri, 20 Nov 2026 04:33:45 UTC (3,285 KB)

items.abstract_original: We are interested in developing a continually self-improving remote sensing agentic system. It should identify and address its capability gaps, retaining the resulting improvements to enhance performance on subsequent tasks. However, existing systems typically rely on fixed toolsets and confine their experience accumulation to re-orchestrating predefined capabilities, constraining both capability expansion and the transfer of improvements across tasks. As the infrastructure for agentic systems, the harness manages tools and workflow knowledge as editable, persistent resources outside the base model. These resources can therefore be updated and reused across tasks without additional post-training. Based on these observations, we propose RemoteEvolver, an external harness for remote sensing agents that drives tool and workflow evolution through execution feedback. With the base model parameters fixed, RemoteEvolver acquires missing specialized tools on demand and distills verified successful execution experience from individual tasks into agent skills that can be reused across tasks. The acquired tools and accumulated skills jointly support planning and execution on subsequent tasks. Experiments on Earth-Bench and OpenEarthAgent-Bench show that RemoteEvolver achieves average accuracy gains of 8.18 and 23.86 percentage points over its initial state when tools are fully available and partially missing. Under the same settings, it also outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by an average of 6.77 and 17.10 percentage points, respectively.

items.summary_en: With base-model parameters fixed, RemoteEvolver acquires missing remote-sensing tools and repairs their interface adapters using execution feedback. Verified tools and continually updated skill.md workflows persist for subsequent task planning and execution. The paper also reports negative far-domain transfer and forgetting, so evolution is not uniformly monotonic.

evidence.quote: Implementation Details. In the main experiments, we use Qwen3.8 27B [ 16 ] as the backbone for all methods except OpenEarthAgent and RemoteAgent, which retain their officially released checkpoints. We further evaluate RemoteEvolver with GPT-5.6 Luna, Qwen3.8 Max [ 16 ] , DeepSeek V4.1 Flash [ 27 ] , MiniMax M3 [ 12 ] , and GLM 5.3 [ 34 ] . Within each method, the same model serves as both the planner and executor. All models operate in thinking mode with the temperature set to 0. We impose no explicit limits on execution steps or output tokens. The tool execution environment is equipped with 8 NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs. More implementation details are provided in Appendix.
evidence.purpose: model and execution-budget limitations

evidence.quote: As shown in Fig. 3 , while the overall accuracy initially rises, subsequent checkpoints reveal a non-monotonic trend. Specifically, while near-domain transfer FWT Near \mathrm{FWT}_{\mathrm{Near}} remains largely positive, far-domain transfer FWT Far \mathrm{FWT}_{\mathrm{Far}} suffers from severe fluctuations, sometimes dropping below 0 on OpenEarthAgent-Bench. Simultaneously, the retention rate abnormally increases, indicating the agent forgets previously mastered tasks. These observations highlight a critical insight: simply expanding the harness does not guarantee stable performance growth . Thus, we conduct a deep analysis and attribute this non-monotonic degradation to a cascading effect across three levels of the agent’s expanded action space: tool exploration, skill retrieval, and workflow execution, as illustrated in Appendix.
evidence.purpose: non-monotonic behavior and negative far-domain transfer

items.title: Physics-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement of Amortized Bayesian Inference Across Physics

identity.submission_history: Submission history From: Bo Liang [ view email ] [v1] Fri, 20 Nov 2026 02:36:12 UTC (237 KB)
identity.hf_date_note: No HF date inferred from an issue, arXiv submission, HTTP last-modified or review date.
identity.first_seen_action: preserve existing canonical value; no first_seen mutation performed

items.abstract_original: Across physics, from the orbits of imaged exoplanets and the matter inside neutron stars to thin films at synchrotrons and cortical neurons, conservation laws, interference, and compensating currents compress the posteriors of precise data into tiny, curved regions where Markov chains need minutes to days. We introduce PhyRSI (physics-guided recursive self-improvement), in which an AI agent coupled to the simulator writes and revises an amortized Bayesian inference algorithm for each field, scored by the importance weights of the exact likelihood because the true posterior is unknown. It evolves coordinates, symmetries, and factorizations matched to the physics: orbital elements at the best-measured epoch, Fresnel-normalized reflectivity with a chart for each of its multiple solutions, coordinates along which Na+ and K+ currents compensate, a shared neutron-star equation of state that factorizes a 32-dimensional joint analysis, and the time-rescaling symmetry of predator-prey dynamics. In six fields, networks trained once on simulations return 36 posteriors of real observations in seconds, reweighted by the likelihood and agreeing with converged Markov chains about as closely as two independent chains agree with each other. Such posteriors could steer synchrotron film growth and patch-clamp recordings as they run, follow X-ray transients while they are bright, update the dense-matter equation of state as neutron stars are added, and compare physical models across catalogs. Inference can thus be evolved and checked by the physics itself rather than designed by hand for each problem.
items.reason_zh: PhyRSI 确有反馈驱动的持久算法演化：代理修改物理问题的坐标、对称性、分解和推断算子代码，利用似然权重及留出模拟检验筛选，再训练并复用科学推断网络。但被改写的是外部科学推断算法这一任务产物；所读全文没有证明代理自己的工具管理、技能、控制流或改进器被反馈改写。因此本轮排除出 Harness 日报，按 ai4ai 保留可恢复记录，而非因训练网络而排除。

items.persistence: Evolved scientific inference algorithms/networks are reused on later observations; this is persistence of a scientific task artifact, not evidenced mutation of the agent Harness.

evidence.quote: AI agent coupled to the simulator writes and revises an amortized Bayesian inference algorithm for each field, scored by the importance weights of the exact likelihood because the true posterior is unknown.
evidence.purpose: actual scientific algorithm update object

evidence.quote: Coupled to the simulator and likelihood, the agent writes an inference algorithm, tests it on sim- ulated observations, reads from the weights why it fails, and rewrites its coordinates, symmetries, and factoriza- tion until it passes the weight check and a calibration test with known parameters on held-out simulations. The re- sult is an amortized algorithm for that field in which a network trained once on simulations (one per planetary system for orbits), combined where needed with a local coordinate chart fitted to the observation, proposes the posterior of any new observation and the exact likelihood reweights and checks it.
evidence.purpose: feedback loop and reuse are confined to inference algorithm

evidence.quote: The loop of Fig. 1 runs on freshly drawn simulated observations, and software blocks any reading of true parameters or reference chains. The agent reads the simulator, the prior, and the statistics of each failure (ESS/M, ˆk, the condition number of the local Hessian, and the rank of the data log-likelihood), works out from the physics of the field why the algorithm fails, and writes the code of a new operator; a candidate is kept only if it passes the check and gives uniform truth-quantile and likelihood ranks on held-out simulated events. Scientists specify the task, the compute budget, and the blinding rules (Supplemental Material). Three classes recur.
evidence.purpose: operator code evolution, failure diagnostics and scientist-fixed task/budget/blinding constraints
